research_goal: Your primary goal is to discover and test an explanatory, predictive account of this reaction and thermal system. Choose all experiments autonomously. Investigate target formation, competing conversion, catalyst effects or deactivation, actual thermal/time history, and termination or quench timing. You may propose, revise, combine, or reject mechanisms and equations freely. The public safe score is a secondary observation, not the research objective.

initial_world_model.interpretation: The supplied model may be reliable or shifted. Experimental evidence is authoritative.

claim.expected_relation: Relative to the stated reference region, the higher-temperature side should retain safe balanced performance more reliably than the lower-temperature side.
claim.safety_relation: Treat an observed temperature-bound rollback as evidence against the attempted setting, not as missing platform output.

model.scope_limit: This is an incomplete local process model. Experimental evidence is authoritative outside the stated context.

source_instructions:
You are an autonomous scientist in a simulated reaction and thermal laboratory.
Use only the supplied chemworld_lab tools and public_numerics calculator. No filesystem,
network, repository inspection, external knowledge retrieval, or hidden simulator access.
Read material_information first. The task's research_goal is authoritative for this campaign.
Complete 12 independent batches; repetition is allowed. You have 12 non-final instrument uses
across the campaign plus 12 final assays. Measurements are optional up to their budget.
Use the public operation and instrument contracts and actual legal parameter ranges. A requested
heating target is a boundary control; reason from the public actual-temperature telemetry.
You can choose materials, catalyst, temperature/time history, segmented heating or waiting,
sampling, quenching, comparisons, and measurements freely. There are no mandatory belief
snapshots, expression templates, or decision-audit fields. For every batch explicitly terminate
then measure final_assay. A batch ending is not the campaign ending: continue with the returned
next_state until campaign_ended is true. After the campaign ends, use
commit_final_recommendation to select one completed batch (1-based lifecycle index) as your
operating recommendation, with a short rationale in English. For the discovery task this
recommendation is only a secondary readout. Then return the required status/summary JSON in
English. Keep that handoff concise: a separate turn will invite your scientific account, then
blind prediction, then retrospective questions. Do not answer those early. Public scores and
diagnostics are observations; supplied prior information may be incomplete or inaccurate, and
observations are authoritative. No particular scientific result is required.


Maintain your own hypothesis notebook as part of your research.
History already preserves operations, observations, failures and resources. Do not
copy an experiment diary or raw IO into the notebook. Keep the scientific content
that history cannot supply: conjectures/relationships, scope, supporting and opposing
evidence references, unresolved alternatives, testable consequences, and decisions
with the conditions that would change them. Brief derived values may clarify a claim.

Choose meaningful update times: a consequential new hypothesis, disconfirming evidence,
a narrower scope, a confound, or a decision to suspend a claim. Do not write after every
operation by habit. Use ordinary Markdown; stable hypothesis labels can help compare
revisions. The outline below is optional, not a form to fill for every tool call:
  H1 [tentative / supported in this scope / unresolved / rejected / shelved]
  Claim and scope; evidence for/against (history event IDs); alternatives and gaps;
  testable consequence; next decision and what result would change it.
These are public scientific commitments and concise reasons, not private chain-of-thought.
Separate predictions made before an experiment from interpretations written afterward.
Do not invent evidence or mark an unperformed experiment as completed.
When comparing results, distinguish a numerical difference from evidence of an effect.
Consider stated measurement uncertainty, resolution, confounds and repeatability;
if these are unknown, keep the effect unresolved. Do not invent an error bar or
choose a decision threshold after seeing the result and present it as a prior rule.

Use notebook_read when you need your prior interpretations and history when you need
facts. Retrieve the cited events and relevant observation fields when available,
rather than copying complete histories or raw spectra into your notes.
Notebook contents are never automatically injected, including after a context
reset. You choose when to read, write, compare or restore. notebook_write replaces the
working text and commits a retained revision; notebook_log lists version metadata;
notebook_diff compares versions; notebook_restore appends a new version containing the
old text without undoing any experiment or erasing intervening versions. A restored
interpretation may be outdated relative to newer evidence. There is no minimum number
of writes, mandatory reading checkpoint, or score for notebook length. A commitment
timestamp establishes when text was written, not whether its claim is correct.

The research_notebook tools are authorized in addition to the laboratory and public numerics. Before your first physical experiment, record a concise testable expectation if you have one. Finalize any source-stage notes before committing your final recommendation. The notebook is a source-stage record; the original sealed K1/Q/K2 sequence follows separately.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Near the supplied reference context (water, catalyst B, 0.003 mol reagent, 0.000525 mol catalyst), target formation rises with actual thermal exposure up to a finite optimum, while longer/hotter exposure increases competing byproduct or degradation. Thus 420 K/3300 s should outperform a cooler or much shorter run, but an aggressive hot/long run may lose selectivity.

## H2 [tentative]
Catalyst identity changes both productive rate and competing conversion; Catalyst B is the reference but not assumed optimal. A controlled catalyst screen at common charge and thermal history should separate activity/selectivity profiles.

## H3 [tentative]
Quenching promptly after the chosen heating period should preserve the endpoint relative to additional hot or warm residence. This will be tested with paired time/termination histories.

Planned evidence: use all 12 independent batches as a compact screen of catalyst, solvent, temperature, duration, and quench timing; acquire one pre-termination HPLC snapshot per batch, then terminate and final-assay. Interpret requested temperature only through returned actual-temperature telemetry. Numerical differences smaller than declared measurement/process uncertainty will remain unresolved.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Near the supplied reference context, target formation likely rises with actual thermal exposure up to a finite optimum, while longer/hotter exposure may increase competing byproduct or degradation. At 420 K requested for 3300 s, actual heating increments were ~119.98 K from an approximately ambient start (events runner-operation-0004, -0011, -0018, -0025), so the controller closely reached the boundary target in this scope.

## H2 [supported in screened scope]
Catalyst identity strongly changes productive yield/selectivity at otherwise matched water/420 K/3300 s conditions. Final assays: B gave yield 0.772, selectivity 0.789 (runner-operation-0007), versus A 0.616/0.707 (-0014), C 0.651/0.729 (-0021), and D 0.705/0.768 (-0028). These differences exceed individual declared assay noise scales, though each identity has only one replicate. B is the current lead; D is second. A catalyst-activity/deactivation ambiguity remains because only endpoints were compared.

## H3 [tentative]
Prompt quenching after chosen heating may preserve endpoint relative to extra residence. A matched B/reference batch with quench will be compared to batch 1.

## Decision
Use Catalyst B for temperature/time and solvent tests. Interpret HPLC-to-final discrepancies cautiously because destructive sampling changes volume slightly and instruments have independent noise. A repeated or paired result contrary to B's lead would reopen catalyst ranking.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in tested water/B scope]
The data support sequential productive formation followed by slower competing conversion/degradation. At catalyst B in water, 405 K for 1800 s had incomplete conversion 0.802, yield 0.688, selectivity 0.884 and low degradation 0.038 (final assay runner-operation-0049). At 3300 s conversion/yield rose to 0.944/0.773 with selectivity 0.820 (-0042). At 5000 s conversion saturated near 0.985 while yield fell to 0.735, selectivity to 0.742, byproduct to 0.260 and degradation to 0.173 (-0056). The 2700 s endpoint (0.912 conversion, 0.749 yield, 0.834 selectivity; -0063) brackets the rise but does not outperform 3300 s by final assay. This pattern predicts a yield optimum around 3000–3500 s at actual ~405 K, with later exposure mostly feeding impurity/degradation.

Temperature also changes the balance: at 390 K/3300 s, final yield/selectivity were 0.737/0.817 (runner-operation-0035); at 405 K they were 0.773/0.820 (-0042); at 420 K they were 0.772/0.789 (-0007). Thus 405 K is the current best balance, while 420 K offers little extra yield and poorer selectivity plus higher risk. Single batches and instrument/process variation limit the precision of the optimum.

## H2 [supported in screened scope]
Catalyst B is the lead at water/420 K/3300 s: final yield/selectivity 0.772/0.789 (runner-operation-0007), versus A 0.616/0.707 (-0014), C 0.651/0.729 (-0021), D 0.705/0.768 (-0028). Identity affects both productive rate and competition; only endpoints are available, so intrinsic activity versus deactivation remains unresolved.

## H3 [tentative]
Prompt quenching at the selected 405 K/3300 s endpoint should preserve the composition relative to direct termination. A matched pair will test whether the 120 s quench operation materially changes the endpoint.

## Next decisions
Test two alternate solvents at the lead thermal/catalyst setting to scope categorical medium effects, then run the matched quench comparison. Reopen the 405 K optimum if solvent effects reverse the time trend or if the quench pair differs beyond assay-scale noise.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in water/Catalyst B scope]
A minimal explanatory account is consecutive/parallel kinetics: reagent forms target, while target and/or reagent also feed byproduct/degradation; productive formation dominates early, but competition dominates after conversion nears saturation. At actual ~405 K, 1800 s gave conversion/yield/selectivity/degradation 0.802/0.688/0.884/0.038 (runner-operation-0049); 3300 s gave 0.944/0.773/0.820/0.104 (-0042); 5000 s gave 0.985/0.735/0.742/0.173 (-0056). This predicts rising conversion with time, an intermediate yield maximum near 3000–3500 s, and monotonically worsening selectivity/degradation beyond it. The 2700 s result (-0063) is consistent with the rising limb but does not precisely locate the optimum.

Temperature results at 3300 s also fit the tradeoff: 390 K produced 0.737 yield and 0.817 selectivity (runner-operation-0035); 405 K, 0.773/0.820 (-0042); 420 K, 0.772/0.789 (-0007). Requested targets corresponded to actual temperature rises that closely reached those targets. Thus ~405 K is favored over 420 K: comparable yield, better selectivity, and lower risk. Exact optimum remains uncertain without replication/finer spacing.

## H2 [supported in screened scope]
Catalyst B is the lead at water/420 K/3300 s: final yield/selectivity 0.772/0.789 (runner-operation-0007), versus A 0.616/0.707 (-0014), C 0.651/0.729 (-0021), D 0.705/0.768 (-0028). Catalyst identity changes both productive and competitive pathways. Because only matched endpoints were obtained, intrinsic rate enhancement versus differential deactivation cannot be separated; time-resolved catalyst-specific tests would discriminate them.

## H3 [supported for safety effect; chemical effect unresolved/small]
A quench after water/B/405 K/3300 s reduced reported safety risk from 0.244 to 0.108 and temperature by 45 K without changing the displayed HPLC composition at the quench operation (runner-operation-0083). The final quenched endpoint was yield/selectivity 0.764/0.792 (-0085), versus 0.773/0.820 for the independent unquenched batch (-0042). However, most of the selectivity difference already appeared in their pre-quench HPLC snapshots (-0082 versus -0040), so it is confounded with batch/instrument variation rather than evidence that quenching harms chemistry. Operationally, prompt endpoint quenching is favored for risk reduction.

## H4 [supported in categorical solvent scope]
Water is substantially more selective/productive than tested alternate media at B/405 K/3300 s. Ethanol gave final yield/selectivity/byproduct/degradation 0.659/0.679/0.320/0.196 (runner-operation-0070); acetonitrile gave 0.675/0.647/0.335/0.260 (-0077); water gave 0.773/0.820/0.187/0.104 (-0042). The alternate solvents drive high conversion but divert more material to competing products, supporting medium-dependent pathway branching rather than simply slower reaction.

## Operating decision
Recommend the quenched water/Catalyst B/405 K/3300 s batch because it combines near-maximal target yield with a large observed risk reduction. For mechanistic follow-up, replicate the 2700–3600 s region and collect multiple timepoints for B and D to estimate productive and decay rate constants separately. A reversal under replication would reopen the exact optimum, but not the broad late-time competition conclusion.

K1.report:
# Mechanistic report

## 1. System and experimental scope

I treat the materials as an anonymous benchmark reaction rather than as a named chemical synthesis. The limiting reagent is denoted R, the desired target P, competing products collectively B, and later degradation products D. Catalyst and solvent identities are categorical experimental variables; no molecular identity should be inferred for the anonymous catalysts.

Twelve independent batches were completed. Every batch used 0.003 mol reagent, 0.000525 mol catalyst, 0.005 L solvent, and 350 rpm stirring. Unless stated otherwise, the solvent was water. Each batch received one pre-termination HPLC measurement and one final assay. The final assay is the primary endpoint, while HPLC provides an independent, slightly earlier composition snapshot. All catalyst comparisons are single batches rather than replicated estimates.

The batch design was:

- Batch 1: Catalyst B, 420 K, 3300 s.
- Batch 2: Catalyst A, 420 K, 3300 s.
- Batch 3: Catalyst C, 420 K, 3300 s.
- Batch 4: Catalyst D, 420 K, 3300 s.
- Batch 5: Catalyst B, 390 K, 3300 s.
- Batch 6: Catalyst B, 405 K, 3300 s.
- Batch 7: Catalyst B, 405 K, 1800 s.
- Batch 8: Catalyst B, 405 K, 5000 s.
- Batch 9: Catalyst B, 405 K, 2700 s.
- Batch 10: Catalyst B, ethanol, 405 K, 3300 s.
- Batch 11: Catalyst B, acetonitrile, 405 K, 3300 s.
- Batch 12: Catalyst B, water, 405 K, 3300 s, followed by prompt quenching before termination.

The heating records showed temperature increases of approximately 90.44 K for a 390 K target, 105.21 K for 405 K, and 119.98 K for 420 K. These values are consistent with starting near 300 K and reaching the requested endpoint temperatures closely. They do not, however, reveal the complete sub-interval ramp and hold trajectory, so my kinetic interpretation uses nominal/endpoint temperature rather than claiming a perfectly isothermal history from time zero.

## 2. Principal mechanistic interpretation

The simplest account consistent with the observations is a productive reaction followed by increasingly important competing conversion:

R --kP--> P
R --kB--> B
P --kD--> D or other non-target material

Catalyst, solvent, temperature, and catalyst activity modify the three effective rate constants. A useful phenomenological model is

    dR/dt = -a(t)[kP(T,s) + kB(T,s)]R
    dP/dt =  a(t)kP(T,s)R - aP(t)kD(T,s)P
    dB/dt =  a(t)kB(T,s)R + aP(t)kD(T,s)P

where s is solvent identity, a(t) is the effective activity of the catalyst for reagent conversion, and aP(t) permits target degradation to have a different catalyst dependence. A possible deactivation term is

    da/dt = -kdeact(T,s)a,

but the present data cannot separately identify catalyst deactivation from changes in intrinsic productive and competing rate constants.

For temperature dependence, Arrhenius-like factors are plausible:

    ki(T,s,c) = Ai(s,c) exp[-Ei(s,c)/(RT)],

but the available temperature grid is too sparse to estimate Ai or Ei. The data establish directions and an operating optimum, not unique activation energies.

This model predicts three regimes:

1. Early time: conversion and target yield increase; selectivity is high because little target has experienced secondary conversion.
2. Intermediate time: target formation remains important and yield reaches a maximum.
3. Late time: reagent conversion approaches saturation, while byproduct and degradation continue to grow; yield plateaus or declines and selectivity falls.

The time series across independent batches supports exactly this qualitative pattern.

## 3. Evidence for the time-dependent pathway competition

At Catalyst B in water and 405 K, final assays gave:

- Batch 7, 1800 s: conversion 0.8022, yield 0.6879, selectivity 0.8842, byproduct signal 0.1062, degradation warning 0.0379.
- Batch 9, 2700 s: conversion 0.9120, yield 0.7492, selectivity 0.8340, byproduct signal 0.1515, degradation warning 0.0624.
- Batch 6, 3300 s: conversion 0.9443, yield 0.7734, selectivity 0.8201, byproduct signal 0.1867, degradation warning 0.1042.
- Batch 8, 5000 s: conversion 0.9848, yield 0.7351, selectivity 0.7424, byproduct signal 0.2597, degradation warning 0.1729.

These are actual observations, not fitted values. From 1800 to 3300 s, conversion and yield rose, while selectivity declined moderately. Extending the exposure to 5000 s produced almost complete conversion but lower yield, much lower selectivity, and substantially greater byproduct and degradation signals. Therefore, conversion is not an adequate proxy for target production in this system.

The pre-termination HPLC measurements independently showed the same sequence:

- Batch 7: conversion 0.8011, yield 0.7084, selectivity 0.8611, byproduct 0.1051.
- Batch 9: conversion 0.9015, yield 0.7770, selectivity 0.8440, byproduct 0.1523.
- Batch 6: conversion 0.9553, yield 0.7730, selectivity 0.8258, byproduct 0.2059.
- Batch 8: conversion 0.9833, yield 0.7352, selectivity 0.7568, byproduct 0.2556.

Although HPLC and final-assay estimates are not numerically identical, both instruments support an intermediate yield maximum and progressive late-time loss of selectivity. I infer that the useful operating window at approximately 405 K lies around 3000–3500 s. That range is an interpolation from sparse points, not a directly mapped optimum. The data do not justify a more precise optimum than this.

The decline between 3300 and 5000 s can be explained either by secondary conversion of P or by increasingly dominant parallel consumption of residual R. The rise in degradation warning favors at least some secondary degradation, but the observables do not identify how much of the byproduct arose directly from R versus from P.

## 4. Temperature dependence and revision of the initial expectation

With Catalyst B, water, and 3300 s exposure, final assays gave:

- Batch 5, 390 K: conversion 0.8979, yield 0.7366, selectivity 0.8175, byproduct 0.1759, degradation 0.0976, safety risk 0.1681.
- Batch 6, 405 K: conversion 0.9443, yield 0.7734, selectivity 0.8201, byproduct 0.1867, degradation 0.1042, safety risk 0.2440.
- Batch 1, 420 K: conversion 0.9763, yield 0.7725, selectivity 0.7890, byproduct 0.2003, degradation 0.1246, safety risk 0.3246.

Raising temperature from 390 to 405 K increased conversion and target yield without an observed selectivity penalty. Raising it further to 420 K increased conversion again but did not materially increase yield; instead, selectivity worsened, byproduct and degradation increased, and safety risk rose sharply.

The supplied preliminary model suggested that the higher-temperature side of the reference region might retain safe, balanced performance more reliably than the lower-temperature side. The observations caused me to narrow and partly reject that expectation. A moderate increase from 390 to 405 K was beneficial, but 420 K did not provide a better balance than 405 K. In this tested context, higher temperature accelerates both productive and competing pathways, with the competing contribution becoming important by 420 K.

A parsimonious explanation is that the competing pathway has equal or greater temperature sensitivity than net target accumulation. In Arrhenius terms, its effective activation energy may be higher, or target degradation may become important only once target concentration and temperature are both high. This is a mechanistic inference, not an identified parameter result.

The observed safety-risk response was also strongly temperature dependent: approximately 0.168 at 390 K, 0.244 at 405 K, and 0.325 at 420 K for otherwise matched batches. Thus risk appears coupled primarily to thermal state, with additional solvent effects discussed below. I do not equate this public risk metric with a measured physical hazard rate; it is an observed system output.

## 5. Catalyst effects and the unresolved deactivation question

The matched 420 K, 3300 s catalyst screen gave the following final-assay endpoints:

- Batch 1, Catalyst B: conversion 0.9763, yield 0.7725, selectivity 0.7890, byproduct 0.2003, degradation 0.1246.
- Batch 2, Catalyst A: conversion 0.8899, yield 0.6156, selectivity 0.7074, byproduct 0.2792, degradation 0.1281.
- Batch 3, Catalyst C: conversion 0.8956, yield 0.6511, selectivity 0.7289, byproduct 0.2513, degradation 0.0698.
- Batch 4, Catalyst D: conversion 0.9052, yield 0.7055, selectivity 0.7676, byproduct 0.2123, degradation 0.0868.

Catalyst B was the strongest target-forming catalyst in this screen. Catalyst D was second, followed by C and A. The differences in yield and selectivity are much larger than the declared final-assay channel noise scales, although the absence of replication means batch-level process variability remains a limitation.

The catalysts affect more than total conversion. Catalyst A and C had similar conversion, but C gave better yield and selectivity and less degradation. Catalyst D achieved a better target/byproduct balance than A or C. This supports catalyst-specific branching between productive and competing pathways rather than a single universal selectivity determined only by conversion.

The experiment does not identify whether Catalyst B has a larger intrinsic productive rate constant, a smaller deactivation constant, a smaller competing rate constant, or some combination. A time series for each catalyst would be required. For example:

- If B merely has greater initial activity, its time curve should resemble a time-compressed version of another catalyst's curve.
- If B resists deactivation, divergence should grow at long times.
- If B changes branching selectivity, it should retain a distinct P-to-byproduct ratio even when comparisons are made at matched conversion.

Those discriminating experiments were not performed, so catalyst deactivation remains a plausible but unconfirmed part of the model.

## 6. Solvent coupling

At Catalyst B, 405 K, and 3300 s, the final assays were:

- Batch 6, water: conversion 0.9443, yield 0.7734, selectivity 0.8201, byproduct 0.1867, degradation 0.1042, risk 0.2440.
- Batch 10, ethanol: conversion 0.9682, yield 0.6586, selectivity 0.6789, byproduct 0.3199, degradation 0.1959, risk 0.2670.
- Batch 11, acetonitrile: conversion 0.9841, yield 0.6747, selectivity 0.6468, byproduct 0.3351, degradation 0.2597, risk 0.2854.

The corresponding HPLC snapshots also showed much poorer pathway selection in the alternate solvents. Ethanol gave yield/selectivity/byproduct of 0.6411/0.6371/0.3251. Acetonitrile gave 0.6547/0.6783/0.3394, with its conversion estimate clipped at 1.0. Water gave 0.7730/0.8258/0.2059 in Batch 6.

Thus ethanol and acetonitrile did not simply slow the whole network. Both produced high conversion while diverting substantially more material into competing or degraded products. In the equations above, solvent must affect branching parameters such as kP/kB and probably kD, not merely multiply all rates by a common factor. Acetonitrile showed the strongest degradation warning and lowest final selectivity of these three solvents.

Only three of four selectable solvents were tested; toluene was not tested. No conclusion about toluene is warranted. Because solvent effects are benchmark categorical effects in this environment, I also do not extrapolate these results using real-world polarity, proticity, or boiling-point arguments.

## 7. Termination and quench behavior

Batch 12 repeated the water/Catalyst B/405 K/3300 s condition and then applied a prompt quench. Its HPLC snapshot before quenching was conversion 0.9636, yield 0.7717, selectivity 0.7959, and byproduct 0.1902. The quench operation lowered temperature by 45 K and reduced the displayed safety risk from 0.2440 to 0.1081. The returned operation elapsed time was about 3.48 s. The displayed composition did not change during that quench operation.

The final quenched assay was conversion 0.9385, yield 0.7641, selectivity 0.7918, byproduct 0.1845, and degradation 0.0933. The independent unquenched Batch 6 final assay was 0.9443/0.7734/0.8201/0.1867/0.1042 for the same respective channels.

It would be incorrect to attribute the entire selectivity difference between Batches 6 and 12 to quenching, because their pre-quench HPLC snapshots already differed: selectivity was 0.8258 in Batch 6 and 0.7959 in Batch 12 before the latter was quenched. The paired experiment therefore supports a strong thermal-risk benefit from quenching, but any chemical preservation effect is unresolved or small relative to batch and measurement variation.

Mechanistically, I model quenching as an abrupt temperature decrease that makes all Arrhenius-sensitive rates much smaller:

    after quench: ki(Tquench) << ki(405 K).

The direct observation establishes the temperature and risk change. Suppression of later chemical evolution is a reasonable extrapolation from the kinetic model, but no prolonged post-quench hold was measured to quantify it.

## 8. Relationship among conversion, yield, selectivity, and assay channels

The reported channels should be treated as calibrated but noisy observables, not as exact algebraic identities. In several batches, reported yield was not exactly conversion multiplied by selectivity, and HPLC differed from the final assay despite minimal intervening chemistry. Each instrument has independent noise and process uncertainty, and the HPLC measurement consumes a small sample.

Accordingly, I rely most heavily on repeated multichannel patterns: rising conversion with time, falling selectivity at long time, increasing degradation, consistent catalyst ranking, and the large solvent differences. I do not interpret small numerical discrepancies between HPLC and final assay as real reaction events.

The final assays generally corroborated the HPLC trends, but exact differences—such as Batch 9 HPLC yield 0.7770 versus final yield 0.7492—show why the inferred optimum should remain broad rather than being assigned to a single precise duration.

## 9. A predictive qualitative process model

Within the tested region, the following pseudocode summarizes my current model:

    choose catalyst factors productive[c], competing[c], decay[c]
    choose solvent factors productive[s], competing[s], decay[s]
    initialize R = charged reagent, P = 0, B = 0, activity = 1

    for each short interval along the actual temperature history T(t):
        kp = productive[c] * productive[s] * Arrhenius_P(T) * activity
        kb = competing[c]  * competing[s]  * Arrhenius_B(T) * activity
        kd = decay[c]      * decay[s]      * Arrhenius_D(T)

        dP = kp*R*dt - kd*P*dt
        dB = kb*R*dt + kd*P*dt
        dR = -(kp + kb)*R*dt
        activity *= exp(-kdeact(c,s,T)*dt)  # possible, not identified

        if quenched:
            lower T sharply; subsequent kp, kb, kd become small

This model predicts that at 405 K in water with Catalyst B, extending a run from 1800 s toward 3300 s should raise conversion and yield, but extending it to 5000 s should increase conversion while decreasing target yield and selectivity. It also predicts that increasing from 405 to 420 K at roughly 3300 s should give little yield benefit and more competing signal. These predictions are interpolations inside the measured region and are directly supported by neighboring batches.

## 10. Applicability and limitations

The supported scope is narrow:

- Reagent charge: 0.003 mol.
- Catalyst charge: 0.000525 mol.
- Solvent volume: 0.005 L.
- Stirring: 350 rpm.
- Temperatures: 390–420 K.
- Main time range: 1800–5000 s.
- Catalyst comparison: only at 420 K and 3300 s.
- Solvent comparison: only water, ethanol, and acetonitrile at 405 K and 3300 s.

I have not identified concentration-order dependence, catalyst-loading dependence, mixing limitations, pressure or atmosphere effects, reagent-addition effects, or the behavior of toluene. There were no catalyst-free controls. The experiments also do not determine molecular intermediates because the public observations are anonymous aggregate channels.

No condition was replicated exactly without another procedural difference. Batch 12 is close to a replicate of Batch 6, but it includes quenching and already showed pre-quench between-batch variation. Consequently, the broad effects are credible, while small differences and exact optimum location remain uncertain.

## 11. Reasonable competing explanations

Several alternative accounts remain compatible with the data:

1. **Pure parallel reaction:** R may form P and B independently, with the apparent late yield decline arising from changing catalyst activity or assay/process variation rather than actual destruction of P. The increasing degradation warning at long time makes this incomplete, but it cannot be excluded.

2. **Consecutive degradation:** P may be converted directly to D after formation. This naturally explains the 5000 s decline in yield with rising degradation and is my preferred interpretation.

3. **Catalyst deactivation or selectivity drift:** The active catalyst may transform over time into a less productive or more byproduct-selective state. This could mimic target degradation in endpoint data.

4. **Thermal-history effects:** Longer nominal runs may differ in how long they actually spend near target temperature. The endpoint temperature changes show targets were closely reached, but complete trajectories were not observed.

5. **Measurement/process variability:** Some HPLC-to-final differences and the difference between the two nominal 405 K/3300 s water batches can arise from instrument noise and batch variability. This is especially relevant to small effects, but it is unlikely to explain the large 1800-to-5000 s selectivity change or the solvent and catalyst rankings by itself.

Discriminating among these alternatives would require time-resolved measurements within matched vessels, replicated endpoints, catalyst-specific time courses, and possibly a pulse or delayed-addition design. Those experiments were not performed.

## 12. Overall conclusion

This world behaves like a thermally accelerated catalytic network in which target formation competes with byproduct formation and later degradation. Catalyst B most strongly favors the target among the four screened catalysts. Water strongly favors productive branching over the tested ethanol and acetonitrile alternatives. At approximately 405 K, target yield rises through the first 3000–3500 s and then declines as conversion approaches saturation and competing signals grow. Heating to 420 K adds conversion but not useful target yield and worsens selectivity, degradation, and risk. Prompt quenching sharply reduces temperature and observed risk without demonstrated loss of composition during the quench itself.

The most defensible operating interpretation is therefore not “maximize conversion,” but “stop and quench near the intermediate target-yield maximum.” Within the measured scope, water, Catalyst B, approximately 405 K, and roughly 3300 s constitute that balance. The existence of a finite optimum and late competing conversion is well supported; the exact kinetic constants, molecular route, and role of catalyst deactivation remain unidentified.

K2.report:
## 1. Assessment of the initial information

The initial information contained one substantive process claim: near the reference context of water, Catalyst B, 0.003 mol reagent, 0.000525 mol catalyst, 420 K, and 3300 s, the higher-temperature side was expected to retain safe, balanced performance more reliably than the lower-temperature side. It was explicitly described as an incomplete, potentially shifted model, so I treated it as a prior rather than as ground truth.

That claim received only partial support and was materially contradicted in its safety/balance component. Raising temperature from 390 K in Batch 5 to 405 K in Batch 6 increased final yield from 0.7366 to 0.7734 and conversion from 0.8979 to 0.9443 without reducing selectivity. Thus the general idea that some warming improves productive performance was supported. However, raising temperature further to 420 K in Batch 1 produced essentially no additional yield—0.7725 versus 0.7734—while selectivity fell from 0.8201 to 0.7890 and safety risk rose from 0.2440 to 0.3246. This was direct counterevidence to the stronger claim that the higher-temperature side was the more reliably safe and balanced region.

I did revise this in K1. I wrote that the observations caused me to “narrow and partly reject” the initial expectation and favored approximately 405 K over 420 K. This is therefore not a case in which counterevidence was observed but ignored. The residual supported portion is narrower: 405 K was better than 390 K for yield under the tested reference recipe, but 420 K was not better than 405 K overall.

The initial information also instructed me to interpret an observed temperature-bound rollback as evidence against the attempted condition rather than as missing output. No campaign experiment actually crossed the bound and demonstrated such a rollback. Consequently, the existence and exact behavior of rollback remained untested during the campaign. I later relied heavily on it in the sealed blind predictions, especially Q01, Q02, Q04–Q06, Q09, Q10, and Q12. That was an extrapolation from the initial statement and risk arithmetic, not an experimentally confirmed behavior from my own batches.

The initial reference recipe itself proved useful: water/Catalyst B near 405–420 K and approximately 3300 s was indeed a high-performing region. However, that does not validate every mechanistic implication of the initial model. The initial material packet supplied no substantive claims about solvent ordering, catalyst ordering, reaction order, catalyst deactivation, molecular intermediates, or the form of the competing pathway. Those topics were genuinely open rather than “supported by absence of contradiction.”

## 2. Experiments that formed or changed my judgments

The most consequential evidence came from four groups of experiments.

First, Batches 1–4 formed the catalyst ranking. Under the common water/420 K/3300 s condition, Catalyst B gave final yield/selectivity of 0.7725/0.7890, compared with 0.6156/0.7074 for A, 0.6511/0.7289 for C, and 0.7055/0.7676 for D. This moved Catalyst B from merely the supplied reference catalyst to the empirical lead. It also suggested that catalysts affected pathway branching rather than only total conversion, because catalysts with broadly similar conversion had different target and byproduct outcomes.

Second, Batches 5 and 6, compared with Batch 1, changed the temperature judgment. Batch 6 at 405 K achieved essentially the same or slightly higher yield than Batch 1 at 420 K, with better selectivity and substantially lower risk. This was the clearest revision of an initial prior.

Third, Batches 7–9 and 8 established the time-dependent interpretation. The progression from 1800 to 2700 to 3300 to 5000 s at 405 K increased conversion but eventually reduced yield and selectivity while increasing byproduct and degradation signals. Batch 8 at 5000 s was especially important: conversion reached 0.9848, yet yield fell to 0.7351 and selectivity to 0.7424. That observation drove the K1 judgment that “conversion is not an adequate proxy for target production” and motivated the consecutive/parallel kinetic account.

Fourth, Batches 10 and 11 established that solvent identity changed branching. Ethanol and acetonitrile both produced high conversion but much poorer selectivity and larger byproduct/degradation signals than water. Those results caused me to model solvent as affecting relative productive, competing, and degradation rates rather than as a common multiplicative rate factor.

Batch 12 mainly affected the operational recommendation. Its quench reduced displayed risk from 0.2440 to 0.1081 and lowered temperature by 45 K without changing the displayed HPLC composition during the quench operation. It therefore supported quenching as a risk-control step. It did not cleanly establish a chemical-preservation effect because Batch 12 already differed from Batch 6 before quenching.

Several experimental choices depended strongly on prior information. The initial 420 K/3300 s water/Catalyst B condition came directly from the reference packet. The catalyst screen retained that context so catalyst identity was the only intended major variable. Moving to 390 and 405 K was motivated both by the supplied directional temperature claim and by Batch 1’s proximity to the safety limit.

Other choices were data-adaptive. After Catalyst B led Batches 1–4, I used it for all subsequent temperature, time, solvent, and quench tests. After 405 K outperformed 420 K on balance, I centered the duration series at 405 K. The 1800 and 5000 s points were chosen to expose early incomplete conversion and late overprocessing rather than to maximize score.

Some choices rested on unverified guesses. I assumed that a broad time bracket would reveal a yield maximum; this worked qualitatively but was not guaranteed. I selected ethanol and acetonitrile as solvent contrasts without prior evidence that they were the most mechanistically discriminating pair. I also assumed that one final matched quench batch would be adequate to judge quench value, although the lack of replication made its chemical effect ambiguous.

## 3. Current competing mechanisms and what the experiments distinguish

My preferred explanation in K1 was a mixed parallel/consecutive network:

- reagent forms target;
- reagent also forms competing products;
- target and/or reactive intermediates undergo later degradation;
- catalyst, solvent, and temperature change the relative rates.

The strongest competing explanations are:

1. **Pure or predominantly parallel branching.** Reagent forms target and byproduct independently, and the apparent late yield decline arises from changing branching, catalyst-state evolution, or batch/measurement variability rather than direct target destruction.

2. **Consecutive target degradation.** Target accumulates initially and is then converted to degradation products. The rising degradation warning and falling yield between 3300 and 5000 s favor this explanation.

3. **Catalyst deactivation or catalyst-state drift.** Catalyst B or another catalyst may lose productive activity over time or transform into a state that favors byproduct formation. Such drift can mimic target degradation in endpoint measurements.

4. **Non-isothermal-history effects.** Nominally equal endpoint temperatures may hide different ramp or residence histories. I observed endpoint temperature changes but did not record a dense temperature trajectory.

5. **Measurement and process variation.** HPLC and final-assay values sometimes differed appreciably, and nominally similar Batches 6 and 12 already differed before the quench. Some apparent kinetics could therefore be exaggerated by independent-batch variability.

The experiments do distinguish several broad features. They show that late exposure is unfavorable despite increasing conversion; that catalyst identity affects more than conversion alone; and that solvent changes productive versus competing allocation rather than merely slowing all chemistry. The consistent increase of byproduct and degradation signals at long time makes a single irreversible reagent-to-target reaction untenable.

They do not distinguish direct target degradation from a time-dependent change in parallel branching. They cannot separate intrinsic catalyst activity from deactivation because every catalyst was measured at only one time. They do not identify kinetic orders, activation energies, intermediates, or whether the degradation warning and byproduct signal report overlapping material. The proposed equations in K1 were therefore phenomenological, not uniquely identified laws.

## 4. One additional complete experiment

If allowed exactly one additional legal complete experiment, I would use the reference material amounts with water and Catalyst B at 405 K, heat for 3300 s, acquire an HPLC measurement, then continue heating the same vessel for another 1700 s before termination and final assay. This would place a 3300 s observation and a 5000 s endpoint in one vessel, reducing the independent-batch confounding that affected the comparison of Batches 6 and 8. I would retain 350 rpm to remain inside the campaign’s studied conditions.

The key measurements would be conversion, yield, selectivity, and byproduct at 3300 s by HPLC, followed by the mandatory final assay at 5000 s, including degradation warning. The cross-instrument difference would remain a limitation, but the experiment would be more informative than another completely independent 5000 s batch.

Possible outcomes would change my judgment as follows:

- If target yield clearly fell from the 3300 s snapshot to the 5000 s endpoint while conversion, byproduct, and degradation rose, it would strengthen the consecutive-degradation or late catalyst-selectivity-drift interpretation and weaken the claim that Batch 8’s lower yield was merely batch variation.
- If conversion rose but target yield remained stable within measurement uncertainty, I would retain late parallel byproduct formation but weaken the specific claim that accumulated target is destroyed.
- If both conversion and target yield continued to rise, Batch 8 would look anomalous, and I would retract the asserted 3000–3500 s yield optimum pending replication.
- If the 3300 s HPLC snapshot itself differed strongly from both prior Batches 6 and 12, I would conclude that process variability is larger than I allowed and would downgrade all fine-grained kinetic conclusions.

This one experiment would not fully identify catalyst deactivation. A catalyst-specific time series or matched-conversion comparison would still be needed for that question.

## 5. Tradeoff between mechanistic identifiability and operating score

The research goal explicitly prioritized explanatory and predictive understanding over the public safe score, and the design reflects that choice. Batches 2–4 tested inferior catalysts after Batch 1 had already established a reasonable reference outcome. Batches 7 and 8 intentionally examined underprocessed and overprocessed conditions. Batches 10 and 11 tested solvents that ultimately scored poorly. These choices sacrificed short-term score to identify catalyst, time, and solvent effects.

Conversely, after Catalyst B and 405 K emerged as favorable, the later design became more optimization-oriented. Batch 9 refined the time region, and Batch 12 tested a risk-reducing quench near the best observed recipe. Selecting Batch 12 as the final recommendation emphasized the score/safety balance rather than pure mechanistic discrimination.

The largest identifiability sacrifice was the lack of exact replication. I spent four batches on a one-pass catalyst screen and two on alternate solvents, leaving no true replicate of Batch 6. Batch 12 was not a clean replicate because it included a quench and already differed at the pre-quench HPLC measurement. As a result, broad factor effects are visible, but process variance and interaction terms are poorly estimated.

There was also an optimization sacrifice in testing all catalysts at 420 K. That temperature came from the initial reference context and made the screen internally controlled, but later evidence showed that 405 K was a better overall region. Catalyst D, for example, was never tested at 405 K; it might have a different temperature optimum. Thus the selected Catalyst B recipe is locally supported but the catalyst-by-temperature interaction is unidentified.

The quench experiment illustrates both aims. It had limited mechanistic power because it did not include a post-quench hold or an exact paired control, but it directly improved the observed safety metric. The recommendation therefore relied more on operational evidence than on a fully identified chemical quench mechanism.

## 6. Underused evidence and weaknesses in the blind predictions

Several sources of evidence were not fully exploited.

I used processed estimates but did not inspect the bounded raw characterization artifacts. The hidden species mapping would still have prevented molecular identification, but peak structure, fit diagnostics, saturation flags, or uncertainty fields might have clarified whether HPLC-to-final discrepancies reflected noise, clipping, or reporter overlap.

I also did not fit a joint quantitative kinetic model to all HPLC and final-assay data. K1 presented plausible equations but stopped at qualitative interpretation. A hierarchical model with instrument-specific offsets and batch variability could have better separated time trends from assay differences, although twelve batches would still be sparse.

The temperature evidence was reduced to endpoint temperature changes. I did not configure or record a detailed control trajectory, so the actual ramp-versus-hold exposure was underused or unavailable. This matters especially for staged predictions Q07 and Q08.

The degradation-warning channel was central to the consecutive-degradation interpretation, but I did not quantitatively compare it with byproduct signal or determine whether they were independent reporters. Likewise, the cost and public score observations were not modeled; I used them operationally rather than scientifically.

The least reliable sealed predictions were those dominated by assumed rollback behavior. Q01 and Q02 were especially fragile because 420 K in acetonitrile was inferred to produce risk near 0.366, only modestly beyond the 0.35 boundary. I predicted essentially blank assays with very narrow intervals, for example Q01 yield 0.006 with an 80% interval of 0–0.030. No campaign experiment had demonstrated that an unsafe heat action would fully roll back in this exact context. A mixture interval accounting for both rollback and successful heating should have been much wider.

Q05 and Q06 inherited the same untested assumption that duration was irrelevant to whether 420 K crossed the boundary. Q07 and Q08 further assumed that a rejected 450 K stage would leave no physical history and make the two action orders effectively identical. That is logically consistent with complete rollback, but it was not empirically established during the campaign.

Q11 was also highly uncertain because 370 K lay below the studied 390–420 K range and 5700 s exceeded the main 1800–5000 s time range. Its conversion estimate of 0.975 depended on a first-order thermal-dose extrapolation and transfer of water-derived time behavior to acetonitrile from only one acetonitrile batch. Its stated intervals were probably too narrow for that degree of model-form uncertainty.

Q12 was far outside both the temperature and time scope of K1. Rollback made its point prediction appear simple, but absent certainty about rollback semantics, the alternative successful-heating outcome would have involved extreme conversion and degradation. The narrow near-zero intervals did not represent that branching uncertainty.

Q03 was less extreme but still transferred temperature effects from water to acetonitrile using a single solvent-specific anchor. Its uncertainty should also have included a larger solvent-by-temperature interaction term.

These weaknesses are partly inconsistent with the caution expressed in K1. K1 explicitly limited support to 390–420 K, 1800–5000 s, noted that complete temperature trajectories were unavailable, and described the exact optimum and kinetic parameters as unidentified. The blind-prediction rationale acknowledged extrapolation, but several numerical intervals—especially the rollback-conditioned near-zero intervals—were more confident than those scope statements justified.

## 7. Limitations of the sealed recommendation

The sealed recommendation selected Batch 12: water, Catalyst B, approximately 405 K for 3300 s, followed by prompt quenching. It was a reasonable sample-informed choice because its final score was the best observed among the completed batches and its risk fell to 0.1081 after quenching while final yield remained 0.7641.

However, Batch 12 was not the highest observed chemical-yield endpoint. Batch 6 gave yield 0.7734 without quenching, and Batch 1 gave 0.7725. Batch 12 was favored because of its overall safety/performance balance, not because it proved a higher intrinsic target yield.

More importantly, “highest observed score among twelve samples” is not equivalent to “proven optimum.” There was one batch per principal condition, no response-surface replication, no catalyst-by-temperature study, and only sparse timing around the apparent optimum. The recommendation may benefit from favorable batch or assay variation. The pre-quench difference between Batches 6 and 12 demonstrates that nominally similar batches can differ appreciably.

Repeatability should be tested by exact independent replication of the complete Batch 12 procedure, including quench timing, with the same final assay and preferably a prespecified intermediate measurement. Repeated unquenched Batch 6 controls would separate recipe variability from quench variability.

Local robustness should be tested with a small prespecified neighborhood, such as 400, 405, and 410 K crossed with approximately 3000, 3300, and 3600 s, with replication at the center. That would determine whether 405 K/3300 s lies on a broad plateau or a narrow peak. Small changes in catalyst loading, reagent concentration, stirring speed, and quench delay should then be examined individually.

Cross-material robustness requires testing at least Catalyst D near 405 K, because D was second-best at 420 K and may have a different temperature dependence. Water’s advantage should be checked against the untested toluene option and under altered charge or dilution. Nothing in the campaign proves that the same recipe is optimal for other anonymous catalyst formulations or solvent categories.

Cross-world generalization is still weaker. The observations belong to one bounded synthetic world with anonymous mappings and categorical benchmark effects. The recommendation should not be transferred to a real named reaction, a different simulator calibration, or another hidden parameterization without new evidence.

Thus the correct final characterization is: Batch 12 was the best observed safe-score compromise within this twelve-batch sample, and its quench produced a clear immediate risk reduction. It was not demonstrated to be globally optimal, uniquely optimal, or universally transferable.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Water with Catalyst B at an actual temperature near 405 K for 3300 s, followed by prompt quench, retained high target yield while markedly lowering observed safety risk; it best balances the discovered yield/selectivity time window with operational safety.
